claims.text: Rapid processing of Mg-containing alloys can produce and preserve metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution-containing microstructures.
The initial Mg-containing alloy has a nearly uniform elemental distribution and minimal intermetallic content.
Thermal exposure causes localized elemental segregation in the metastable solid solution.
Localized segregation drives a nucleation-and-growth transformation.
Annealing a non-equilibrium solid solution can cause phase decomposition and formation of intermetallic compounds beginning near 800 °C.
Thermal exposure produces Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates in the Mg-containing alloy.
Thermally induced intermetallic phases form both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The intermetallic precipitates cause elemental partitioning and alter local alloy chemistry.
Accelerated diffusion during thermal exposure causes the proposed segregation.
Ti-rich precipitates can promote formation of a continuous, dense TiO2-rich passivating surface film.
A continuous TiO2-rich film retains corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermal exposure can coarsen existing grain-boundary intermetallic phases.
Coarse or heterogeneous precipitation depletes protective elements such as Ti from the matrix.
Depletion of Ti from the matrix or precipitate coarsening compromises passivation and increases susceptibility to corrosion and oxidation.
A uniform, fine precipitate dispersion will produce lower corrosion current density than the unaged metastable baseline.
A uniform, fine precipitate dispersion will produce more stable high-temperature oxide scales than the unaged baseline.
Coarse, inhomogeneously distributed precipitates will increase corrosion rates and compromise oxide-scale integrity.
Temperatures of at least about 800 °C and exposures extending to 1000 hours are sufficient to access diffusion-driven microstructural transformations.
The controlled comparison will age initially equivalent samples at 800, 1000, and 1200 °C for durations up to 1000 hours and compare them with the unaged baseline.
Absence of significant precipitate formation, or absence of any association between precipitate evolution and corrosion or oxidation performance, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
